name: Whitening mouth rinse

lead: Whitening rinses are over-the-counter mouthwashes containing a peroxide, used to lighten tooth colour and reduce surface stain with very little effort.

The peroxide oxidises stain molecules on the teeth, though contact time is short compared with strips or trays, so results are described as gradual. Published work on rinses is mostly laboratory studies, case reports and product analyses rather than clinical trials of cosmetic whitening.

paras: Users swish the rinse as part of the daily routine, twice daily for about a minute each time in the usual description. Visible results can take up to three months.
One case report documents a chemical gum burn after misuse. Peroxide at 10 percent or more is described as able to burn tissue, and EU retail products are limited to 0.1 percent hydrogen peroxide.

angle.text: A peroxide rinse contacts the teeth twice a day and gradually lifts surface stain, giving a slightly brighter smile over weeks to a few months. It is the lowest-effort whitening option; supporting research is mainly laboratory work.

lead: Whitening mouth rinses are over-the-counter mouthwashes, usually containing a low concentration of peroxide or other whitening agents, intended to lighten tooth colour and reduce surface stain. People use them as the lowest-effort way to brighten a smile: swish for about a minute, twice a day, as an add-on to brushing, or to help hold a shade after stronger whitening.[1][2] Wikipedia lists rinses alongside strips, brush-on gels, whitening toothpastes and trays as at-home options, with rinses used twice daily for one minute and visible improvement taking up to three months.[1]

Tooth whitening in general works by chemically breaking down chromogens, the colour-causing compounds in or on the tooth; hydrogen peroxide, or carbamide peroxide which releases it in water, is the main active ingredient, and its free radicals split pigment molecules into smaller, less coloured pieces.[1] Because a rinse is swished rather than held against the teeth, peroxide contact time is brief compared with strips or trays.[1]

Evidence for rinses consists mostly of laboratory studies on extracted or bovine teeth and restorative materials, plus case reports and product analyses, rather than clinical trials of cosmetic whitening.

paras: Whitening rinses are swished in the mouth rather than held against the teeth, so peroxide contact time is brief compared with strips or trays.[1] Wikipedia describes strips as typically used twice daily for 30 minutes over 14 days and trays as worn overnight or for two to four hours a day, in contrast to the one-minute rinse.[1] Whitening toothpastes rely more on abrasives and detergents, with some containing low-concentration peroxide.[1]

A laboratory study of whitening rinses tested a peroxide product (Rembrandt Plus) against alcohol-containing and alcohol-free mouthwashes on bleached composite resin.[3] Other formulations use phosphates or hydroxyapatite rather than peroxide; an in vitro study compared a hydroxyapatite gel with a phosphate-containing whitening rinse and distilled water on enamel samples.[4]

In a 2017 in vitro study, 120 stained bovine enamel-dentin specimens were whitened or not with 10% carbamide peroxide and then cycled through staining and rinsing for 12 weeks; groups using two commercial whitening rinses showed greater colour change than controls, while a bromelain-papain rinse resembled deionized water.[5] A study using bovine teeth bleached with 22% carbamide peroxide found that whitening toothpaste plus whitening rinse maintained colour better than the control after simulated toothbrushing and rinsing, and that perceived whitening was greater than the measured colour change.[6]

In a human-enamel study, a whitening rinse used alone, and in combination with 38% hydrogen peroxide or 10% carbamide peroxide, produced statistically significant colour change versus control; other groups also showed decreases in microhardness and increases in roughness, though the rinse-only group did not decrease microhardness.[7] A comparison of four over-the-counter products with a dentist-prescribed home system also examined microhardness, roughness, colour and bond strength.[8] A laboratory analysis of 16 commercial whitening products compared real and declared hydrogen peroxide concentrations.[9]

Wikipedia places rinses among the at-home options alongside strips, brush-on gels, whitening toothpastes and trays, with rinses typically used twice daily for one minute and visible improvement described as taking up to three months.[1] Because they are easy to add to a routine, people also use them as maintenance after stronger whitening; a 2022 bovine-tooth study found that whitening toothpaste plus whitening rinse maintained colour after bleaching better than control.[6] A 2017 operative dentistry study examined rinses used alone and together with carbamide peroxide home whitening.[5]

The UK National Health Service says whitening chemicals are very strong and should only be used or sold by dental professionals, recommends dental surgeries over beauty salons, and describes dentist-prescribed tray kits worn for around two to six weeks, with an effect that may last around three years with dentist advice; the page does not discuss whitening mouthwashes.[10] It lists tooth sensitivity, sore gums or throat and white patches on the gums as possible side effects of professional whitening.[10] Wikipedia describes retail limits of 0.1 percent hydrogen peroxide in the EU, with higher concentrations allowed under dental supervision, and the US FDA as endorsing gels up to 6 percent hydrogen peroxide.[1]

No studies found of whitening mouth rinses in clinical trials on volunteers. Related laboratory work has examined how whitening rinses affect the surface hardness, gloss and colour of bleached composite resin, bulk-fill composites, and composite aligner attachments stained with coffee and wine.[3][11][12] The enamel and bovine-tooth studies above are in vitro.

A case report described a chemical burn to the gum after misuse of an over-the-counter whitening mouthwash.[2] Wikipedia notes that hydrogen peroxide at 10 percent or more can cause chemical burns, and that EU retail products are limited to 0.1 percent hydrogen peroxide, with up to 6 percent allowed under dental professional supervision.[1] Tooth sensitivity is described as the most common side effect of whitening, with home bleaching following manufacturer instructions causing less than in-office bleaching, and gum irritation and rebound shade loss as teeth rehydrate are also listed.[1] The US FDA is described as endorsing gels up to 6 percent hydrogen peroxide or 16 percent or less carbamide peroxide.[1]

Wikipedia traces whitening from ancient Roman urine-and-goat-milk preparations through acid treatments in the late 17th century, a Pyrozone mouthwash in the late 1920s, and peroxide gels in the 1940s and 1950s, with custom tray bleaching introduced by Dr William Klusmeier in the late 1960s.[1] More than 100 million Americans are reported to have used whitening methods, with spending of about $15 billion in 2010.[1]
